analysis.one_liner: Permanently bans offshore oil and gas drilling along the Atlantic coast and the Straits of Florida.
analysis.headline: Introduced by 18 senators, the bill never got a hearing or a vote and died in committee at the end of the 116th Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would write a permanent ban into law on new oil and gas leasing in four federal offshore areas: the North Atlantic, Mid-Atlantic, South Atlantic, and the Straits of Florida near Florida's coast. Today, whether these waters are opened to drilling is largely up to whoever is Interior Secretary; the bill would take that off the table permanently. Its stated aim is to protect Atlantic and Florida coastlines from oil spills and the drilling infrastructure that comes with them.
analysis.who_benefits: Coastal communities, tourism businesses, and commercial and recreational fishing interests along the Atlantic and Florida coasts, who would be spared the risk of oil spills and the pipelines, platforms, and seismic surveys that offshore drilling brings. Beach towns and seafood economies depend on clean water and coastlines for their livelihoods.

how_it_helps.text: Permanently prohibits the Interior Department from issuing any lease or authorization to explore for, develop, or produce oil, natural gas, or other minerals in the North Atlantic, Mid-Atlantic, South Atlantic, and Straits of Florida planning areas.
Because the ban is written into the Outer Continental Shelf Lands Act rather than set by administrative policy, it could not be reversed by a future administration's offshore leasing plan.
The protected areas cover the populated Atlantic seaboard and waters off Florida, where coastal tourism and fisheries would bear the damage if a spill occurred.

analysis.who_pays: Oil and gas companies would lose access to any new drilling acreage in the Atlantic and the Straits of Florida, and the federal government would forgo whatever lease revenue those areas might have generated. Opponents of offshore drilling bans generally argue that locking up domestic resources could raise energy costs and reduce energy security, though those areas currently produce little or no oil and gas.

drawbacks.text: The bill permanently removes potential domestic oil and gas resources from development, which critics of drilling restrictions argue reduces future energy supply and federal leasing revenue.
The bill does nothing about the Gulf of Mexico, where nearly all U.S. offshore drilling actually happens, so it would not reduce overall offshore production or spill risk nationwide.
A permanent statutory ban forecloses any future compromise if technology, economics, or energy needs change, rather than leaving the decision to periodic review through the offshore leasing process.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The protection is real for the specific coastlines covered: a major spill off Atlantic beaches or the Florida coast would devastate tourism and fishing economies that have no comparable alternative income. The cost to the oil and gas industry is the loss of speculative future acreage in waters where little drilling is occurring today, so the near-term cost to consumers is small. The main honest objection is the rigidity of a permanent ban, but given that a single accident could inflict permanent damage on coastal economies, the trade-off favors protection.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never took it up; it sat there until the Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Senator Menendez introduced the bill with 17 original cosponsors, all Democrats or allied Independents including Senator Sanders.
It was read twice and referred to the Committee on Energy and Natural Resources on the day of introduction, May 2, 2019.
No further action was ever recorded: no hearing, no committee vote, no floor vote, through the end of the 116th Congress on January 3, 2021.

The bill's subject areas — the Atlantic coast and the Straits of Florida — match where 2019 offshore leasing proposals had drawn opposition from coastal states, but the bill never advanced to a vote in either chamber.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil and gas companies benefited from the inaction, since Atlantic and Straits of Florida waters remained open to possible future leasing under whichever offshore plan the Interior Department adopted. Coastal communities got no new legal protection; the moratoria that existed remained a matter of administrative policy rather than law.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Oil and gas companies and drilling interests

for.name: Sen. Robert Menendez
for.role: U.S. Senator from New Jersey; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the COAST Anti-Drilling Act to permanently ban Atlantic and Straits of Florida offshore drilling.

for.name: Sen. Dianne Feinstein, Sen. Cory Booker, Sen. Ed Markey, Sen. Bernie Sanders, and 13 other Democratic and Independent senators
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction; no Republican senator joined.

for.name: Coastal communities and tourism and fishing interests along the Atlantic and Florida coasts
for.role: Stakeholders supporting a permanent drilling ban
for.what_they_did: Groups like these are the bill's named beneficiaries; no formal outside support appears in the congressional record for this bill.

against.name: Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on May 2, 2019 and never held a hearing, markup, or vote on the bill through the end of the Congress.

against.name: Sen. Lisa Murkowski
against.role: Chair of the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for consideration during the 116th Congress, keeping it from any committee or floor vote.

against.name: Senate Republicans
against.role: Majority party controlling the Senate floor and committee agenda in the 116th Congress
against.what_they_did: No Republican cosponsored the bill, and the Senate majority never brought it to the floor.

sides.party_line_note: Every sponsor and cosponsor was a Democrat or Independent — 16 Democratic senators plus Independent Bernie Sanders joined sponsor Menendez — and no Republican ever supported it, while Senate Republicans controlled the agenda.

industries.note: The bill would bar the industry from any new leasing, exploration, or production in the Atlantic and Straits of Florida planning areas. Its opposition to the ban runs against the interests of coastal communities that depend on clean water, since drilling revenue comes at the risk of spill damage to beaches and fisheries.
A permanent ban protects the beaches and clean water that beach towns and tourist economies depend on. A single major spill could inflict long-lasting damage on these businesses.
The bill would keep seismic survey vessels, drilling platforms, and potential spills out of productive Atlantic fishing grounds. Fisheries would bear the brunt of any contamination.

industries.industry: Offshore drilling services and seismic survey contractors
industries.note: Companies that supply drilling rigs, seismic mapping, and offshore services would lose any future Atlantic market. Their work generates the spill and noise risks the ban addresses.
